North Tel Aviv: Neighborhoods, New Projects and Apartment Prices

North Tel Aviv

North Tel Aviv at a glance

North Tel Aviv is one of the most sought-after, most stable and most intricate parts of the Israeli housing market. It is not one neighborhood but a broad, continuous stretch of city: long-established streets and luxury enclaves, urban renewal sites, schools and cultural institutions, green belts, the sea close by and serious transport links. Within it sit Ramat Aviv in all its parts, Neve Avivim, Shikun Lamed, the Old North, Bavli and the emerging Sde Dov quarter. Each has its own character, pace of change and price level, yet together they form the Tel Aviv neighborhoods most closely identified with settled, well-established living.

Demand rests on location, quality of life and a genuine shortage of open land. The beach, Yarkon Park, Tel Aviv University, Ramat Aviv Mall, the main roads and the big employment centers are all within reach, which draws families, move-up buyers, investors, buyers living abroad and the luxury market alike. Alongside older apartments in long, low "railroad" blocks and low-rise buildings, the area is seeing new projects, TAMA 38 (the national plan for strengthening older buildings, in which a developer reinforces the structure and adds apartments), pinui-binui (evacuation and rebuilding: old buildings demolished and replaced) and large-scale planning in the Sde Dov quarter, where about 16,000 apartments are planned. So a real guide to North Tel Aviv real estate has to connect each neighborhood with transport, projects, law, tax and prices.

Ramat Aviv guide (in Hebrew) The Sde Dov quarter (in Hebrew)

  • The neighborhoods Ramat Aviv, Neve Avivim, Shikun Lamed, the Old North, Bavli and the Sde Dov quarter.
  • Flagship project Hagag Group's projects on Einstein Street: 515 apartments in six residential buildings, EINSTEIN TOWER among them.
  • Getting around The planned Green Line of the light rail with its Einstein station, Namir Road and the Ayalon highway.

North Tel Aviv pairs long-established neighborhoods with a wave of new construction, and that is where the price gaps between older stock and new projects come from.

If you are looking to buy an apartment in North Tel Aviv, separate the markets that share one map: resale of older apartments, urban renewal on in-demand streets such as Einstein, new building in Ramat Aviv and its neighbors, luxury in Bavli and around Yarkon Park, and the market of the future in the Sde Dov quarter (in Hebrew). Price gaps between them can be wide even over short distances. An older apartment on a quiet Neve Avivim street is nothing like a new one in a tower on the Einstein corridor, and a home in a luxury project by the park is nothing like a family apartment in an older Green Ramat Aviv building.

The neighborhoods of North Tel Aviv, from Ramat Aviv to Sde Dov

The name North Tel Aviv is used both broadly and narrowly. In the broad sense it covers the urban strip north of the city center up to the Herzliya border, from the sea east to the Ayalon highway and Namir Road. In the usual real estate sense it means a continuous run of established neighborhoods: Ramat Aviv Aleph, Ramat Aviv Bet, Ramat Aviv Gimel, Green Ramat Aviv, Neve Avivim, Shikun Lamed, Bavli, parts of the Old North, the areas around Tel Aviv University and Ramat Aviv Mall, and the new sites of Sde Dov. For a closer look at Ramat Aviv on its own, see our Ramat Aviv guide (in Hebrew).

Ramat Aviv is one of the area's main anchors, and in practice it divides into several sub-areas, each drawing a different crowd. The original Ramat Aviv is known for relatively low-rise building, leafy streets, schools and the university next door. Ramat Aviv Gimel is associated with more modern construction, an affluent population and high price levels. Green Ramat Aviv keeps a quiet, family, neighborhood feel, with easy access to schools and open space. Ramat Aviv Bet and Neve Avivim form an older, sought-after and well-established residential stretch where urban renewal carries growing weight.

Neve Avivim, built in the 1960s and 1970s, is one of the neighborhoods most closely tied to family life in North Tel Aviv. It is known for a quiet, green, settled character: calm inner streets, older apartment buildings, Ramat Aviv Mall and Ramat Aviv Gimel nearby, and easy access to the university and the main roads. In recent years it has become an active arena of urban renewal. On Yehuda HaNasi Street, for example, a plan approved in 2023 replaces five buildings holding 80 apartments with three buildings of up to 14 floors and 195 apartments. Projects like this renew the housing stock step by step while keeping the neighborhood's quiet character.

Shikun Lamed, in the north-west of Tel Aviv, has the sea, the former Sde Dov airfield, Ramat Aviv and the main routes out of the city all close by. It is popular with families who want a relatively quiet setting that is still near the busy centers of the north. Bavli has a different identity: an older, upscale neighborhood beside Yarkon Park and Namir Road, with new projects at a high price level and buyers who want urban quality of life, the park on their doorstep and quick access to central Tel Aviv and the north of the city.

The Old North is the transition zone between classic Tel Aviv and the established north. It is denser and more urban, closer to the city center and the beach, with a mix of older apartments, renovated buildings, shopping streets and an unmistakably Tel Aviv character. For some buyers it is the more urban alternative to Ramat Aviv and Neve Avivim, especially when the beach, restaurants, culture and street life matter more than parking, quiet and green courtyards.

The Sde Dov quarter is the newest chapter of North Tel Aviv. On the site of the former airfield, a large urban quarter is planned with about 16,000 apartments, mixed uses, public buildings, parks, shops, hotels and transport infrastructure. It redraws North Tel Aviv: it adds substantial housing supply where open land has all but run out, and it links Ramat Aviv, Shikun Lamed, the beach, the Reading complex and the northern end of Ibn Gabirol. Anyone weighing North Tel Aviv for the long term has to factor in the effect of Sde Dov on prices, transport, open space and competition among new projects.

Our guides to the neighborhoods of North Tel Aviv: the Old North (in Hebrew), which is Rova 3, west of Ibn Gabirol; Rova 4 (the New North), around Kikar HaMedina, "State Square", home of the Kikar HaMedina Towers; Bavli (in Hebrew); Miriam HaHashmonait (in Hebrew); and Shikun Lamed (in Hebrew).

Character and quality of life in North Tel Aviv

North Tel Aviv is seen as an established place to live because it brings together advantages that rarely share one patch of city: relative quiet, greenery, easy access, good schools, the sea, Yarkon Park, strong public institutions and a varied stock of apartments. Unlike the dense neighborhoods of central Tel Aviv, much of the north was laid out around wider streets, open spaces, courtyards, public buildings and footpaths. That suits families especially well, and also older residents, buyers living abroad and anyone looking for stability in property.

Green is central to the area's identity. Yarkon Park to the south, the coastline to the west, neighborhood gardens, mature trees and quiet streets feel quite unlike the crowded city center. In Ramat Aviv, Neve Avivim and Shikun Lamed, a street's value is measured not only by the distance to the sea or the building's specification, but also by the space between the buildings: sidewalks, trees, public buildings, a school nearby, parking, quiet, shade and everyday services within reach.

For all its calm, North Tel Aviv is not a suburb. It is a city district inside Tel Aviv, with a major mall, a university, shops, cafés, cultural institutions, hospitals and employment centers nearby, and links to the city center, Herzliya, Ramat Gan, Givatayim and the rest of the metropolitan area. The Green Line of the light rail, planned along Ibn Gabirol with an Einstein station, is expected to strengthen the area's connections and change how buyers and investors value being close to a station.

Quality of life here also comes from the social fabric. Some neighborhoods have a very long-standing population alongside young families arriving with urban renewal projects. In Ramat Aviv and Neve Avivim, demand comes from families looking for strong schools, a quiet community and easy access to services. In Bavli and parts of the Old North, it comes from luxury buyers, move-up buyers and residents who want the park and the city center close. Sde Dov is expected to draw new residents gradually, people looking for new construction, modern planning, the beach and a brand-new urban quarter.

The anchors: Tel Aviv University, Ramat Aviv Mall and Yarkon Park

Tel Aviv University

Tel Aviv University is one of the most important anchors in the north of the city. It shapes housing demand, the movement of people, the rental market, the image of the area and the services around it. Living near the campus appeals to students, faculty, families, investors and landlords. Around the university are cultural institutions, libraries, museums, research centers and open spaces, and it ties together Ramat Aviv, Neve Avivim, Ramat Aviv Gimel and the main transport routes.

For buyers, being close to the university is about more than convenience. In some areas it supports steadier rental demand, adds daily activity, widens the range of services and reinforces North Tel Aviv's reputation for education, culture and an upper-middle-class population and above. That said, streets right next to busy hubs can be livelier, so check noise, traffic, parking and neighboring land uses on the ground.

Ramat Aviv Mall

Ramat Aviv Mall is a major commercial and social anchor. It serves Ramat Aviv, Neve Avivim, Shikun Lamed, the university area and other neighborhoods in the north of the city. For many buyers, having the mall nearby raises everyday convenience: shopping, services, cafés, supermarkets, banks, stores and private medical clinics. In a market where daily convenience often translates into a price premium, a major mall within walking distance or a short drive is a real advantage.

On the other hand, living too close to the mall's access roads can mean heavier traffic and tighter parking at certain hours. So when you analyze a property in North Tel Aviv, distinguish between convenient proximity and a location exposed to congestion. An apartment on a quiet inner street near the mall can enjoy both worlds, convenience and calm. One on a busier road calls for a careful look at noise, parking garage entrances, public transport and foot traffic.

Yarkon Park

Yarkon Park is one of North Tel Aviv's most valuable assets. It gives the neighborhoods around it wide green space, walking and cycling paths, sports areas, community facilities, open lawns and a rare urban view. Bavli sits right beside the park, and parts of the Old North enjoy it every day too. For families, dog owners, runners and anyone who wants city life with room to breathe, the park weighs heavily in the decision to buy.

The park also shapes the luxury market. Apartments with open views, close to the Yarkon, newly designed and finished to a high specification, can be priced above ordinary residential neighborhoods. Around Bavli, and in luxury projects such as Park Bavli, the luxury market runs on its own considerations: the view, privacy, the tower, building services, parking, storage, balconies, specification, the developer's reputation and the quality of future building management. There is more on this market in our guide to luxury apartments in Tel Aviv (in Hebrew).

New projects and urban renewal in North Tel Aviv

Urban renewal in North Tel Aviv is moving on three fronts. The first is individual TAMA 38 projects in older buildings, mainly in Neve Avivim, Ramat Aviv and parts of the Old North. The second is larger demolish-and-rebuild projects or multi-building sites, which add new apartments, parking, elevators, safe rooms (the reinforced room Israelis call a mamad) and sometimes retail space. The third is large-scale planning of whole quarters, above all the Sde Dov quarter (in Hebrew), which will add a large mass of new construction where demand is high and supply is limited.

One of the most prominent renewal hubs is Einstein Street in Ramat Aviv. The street connects shopping, housing, public institutions and transport routes, and it benefits from being close to Ramat Aviv Mall, the university and the planned Einstein station of the Green Line. It has its own page, Einstein Street (in Hebrew), but even at the scale of the whole area it has clearly become one of the most important new-construction corridors in North Tel Aviv.

Hagag Group's projects on Einstein Street are the clearest example of how the scale of building here has changed. The company's January 2026 figures put them at six residential buildings with 515 apartments, a shopping center of about 11,400 m², a public building of about 3,950 m² and an underground parking garage with 957 spaces, with a total value estimated at about ₪4 billion. EINSTEIN TOWER, one of the projects in the complex, has 215 apartments in a 28-floor tower and two 13-floor buildings above a commercial base, and the company estimates completion in the third quarter of 2030. The architect is Moshe Tzur. The complex brings together homes, shopping, height, transport and a new image for Einstein Street, so its influence reaches well beyond the apartments themselves.

Alongside them, Ashdar Einstein, whose sales opened in 2021, has three 8-floor buildings with about 45 apartments. Other developers active in the area include Azorim and Shikun & Binui. For buyers, Einstein Street and its surroundings are no longer just an older residential area but a place in transition: from old construction to new, from a neighborhood street to a city artery, and from neighborhood prices to those of a new project in a strategic location.

Apartment prices in North Tel Aviv by neighborhood

Apartment prices in North Tel Aviv are anything but uniform. Even within one neighborhood there can be wide gaps between an older apartment without an elevator, one after TAMA 38, one in a new building, a garden apartment, a penthouse or an apartment in a luxury tower. In the first quarter of 2026, the median deal price for a 4-room apartment (Israelis count the living room, so this is a living room and 3 bedrooms) was ₪5,370,100 in Neve Avivim and its surroundings, ₪6,549,400 in Bavli and ₪8,425,800 in Shikun Lamed (Tochnit Lamed in the official deal data), against ₪5,229,800 across Tel Aviv-Yafo. A median is a whole-apartment price at the midpoint of the deals, not a price per m². Per m², deals in Ramat Aviv in mid-2026 closed at around ₪55,000 on average, in Ramat Aviv Gimel at about ₪51,000 to ₪53,000, and most new projects in Sde Dov stand at around ₪70,000. The gaps reflect location, floor, view, specification, parking, balconies, the developer's reputation and the delivery date.

The luxury market, mainly around Bavli and in projects such as Park Bavli, is priced higher still. There a buyer pays not only for floor area but for the tower, building services, the view, the park, easy parking, the lobby, upkeep, privacy and status. In older neighborhoods such as Neve Avivim, parts of Ramat Aviv and the Old North, price is also shaped by renewal potential: a building advancing a TAMA 38 or pinui-binui project may be priced differently from a similar building with no process under way.

To judge a deal, the price per m² is not enough. Work out the total price, financing, purchase tax (mas rechisha, the Israeli tax on buying property), professional fees, indexation, moving, renovation, future management fees and parking or storage if not included. For a significant purchase here, start with our guides to purchase tax for foreign residents and mortgages for non-residents, and an early legal review by a real estate lawyer (in Hebrew).

Comparing the North Tel Aviv neighborhoods

Neighborhoods in North Tel Aviv are best compared by way of life, not by price alone. A family with children may prefer a quiet street in Ramat Aviv or Neve Avivim, even if the apartment is older. A couple looking for an urban apartment near the sea may lean toward the Old North. A luxury buyer after a tower, a view and building services may focus on Bavli. An investor or long-term buyer may judge Sde Dov by its future stages of development.

The time horizon matters too. If you need a home to live in now, you will judge the surroundings as they are: school, kindergarten, parking, noise, the commute, being near parents or grown children. If you are buying off-plan or in a renewal project, you are also judging the future: building permits, construction stages, the Sale Law guarantee that protects your payments to the developer, development around the site, future transport and nearby projects. A table helps, but it does not replace a specific check of the street, the building and the contract.

Transport and access: light rail, Namir Road and the Ayalon

Transport is one of the main drivers of property values in North Tel Aviv. The area has good access to Namir Road, the Ayalon highway, the east-west routes, Tel Aviv University, Herzliya, Ramat Gan and the city center. For drivers, Namir Road and the Ayalon matter most. For anyone planning to rely on public transport, the Green Line of the light rail changes the picture of future access.

The Green Line is planned to run along Ibn Gabirol, with an Einstein station, linking the north of the city to central Tel Aviv and other employment centers. A station does not add the same value on every street. An apartment within an easy walk of one may see stronger demand, especially from renters and buyers who would rather depend less on a car. An apartment right next to infrastructure works, a busy road or intensive retail calls for a look at noise, congestion, parking and pedestrian flow.

Transport is not only travel time. It shapes daily life, rental value, how well an apartment suits a family and how easy it will be to rent out later. In Ramat Aviv and Neve Avivim, many buyers want quiet inner streets with fast access to the main roads. In Bavli, Namir Road and the Ayalon are an advantage for commuters to employment centers across the metropolitan area. In Sde Dov, future transport will be integral to the quarter's success, because a new quarter of about 16,000 apartments has to rely on public transport, walking and cycling paths and efficient street planning.

Who North Tel Aviv suits

North Tel Aviv suits, first and foremost, families looking for a stable place to live, good schools, green space and easy access. Ramat Aviv, Neve Avivim and Shikun Lamed fit this group especially well when the priority is a quiet street, schools, community, gardens and day-to-day convenience. Families from other parts of Tel Aviv, or from Herzliya, Ramat HaSharon and Ra'anana, sometimes see North Tel Aviv as a more urban but still relatively quiet alternative. If you are comparing it with Herzliya, see also our page on new projects in Herzliya (in Hebrew), including Herzliya Pituach.

The area also suits move-up buyers. Many buyers here are not buying a first home but trading up to one that is larger, newer or closer to the park, the sea or the schools. For them, the key question is not just the price per m² but long-term fit: the number of rooms, the layout, an elevator, parking, storage, a safe room, a balcony, the floor, the view, upkeep, the house committee and the street.

Investors look at North Tel Aviv with a different kind of caution. Entry prices are high, so the ongoing rental yield may be lower than in cheaper areas. On the other hand, this is a sought-after, stable market with rental demand from families, students, academics, residents from abroad and people working in the employment centers. It usually suits those seeking stability, preservation of value, renewal potential or a quality long-term holding, rather than a high running yield.

Buyers living abroad and luxury buyers are drawn mainly by the sea, the park, the future Sde Dov quarter (see our page on Rainbow in Sde Dov), Bavli and new projects with a high specification. For them, building management, security, parking, access to the airport, nearby hotels, services in English or French and the ability to look after the apartment from a distance carry real weight. Here too, separate an apartment for occasional stays from one to rent out, and a luxury tower apartment from an older apartment in a quiet neighborhood.

Legal and tax points before you buy

Buying in North Tel Aviv calls for careful legal and tax checks, especially with a new project, urban renewal, an off-plan purchase or an expensive property. Where prices are this high, even a small mistake in the contract, the handover, the attached parking or storage, the tax or the property rights can be costly. So the review should start not on the day of signing, but when you choose the property and weigh the risk.

For a resale apartment, check the registration of rights, the Tabu extract (the land registry record) or a confirmation of rights, attached parking and storage, building violations, actual use, planning status, building rights, debts to the municipality, a possible betterment levy, the building's condition, neighbors' consents and any urban renewal process. An ordinary-looking older building may be part of a TAMA 38 or pinui-binui process, but not every such process reaches construction. There is a big difference between an initial idea, partial signatures, a chosen developer, a permit application, a conditional permit, a full permit and bank financing of the project.

When buying from a developer, check the developer's identity, the status of the land, the building permit, timelines, the technical specification, indexation terms, guarantees, cancellation terms, changes to the apartment, service areas, parking, storage, management fees, the condominium bylaws, common areas and any commercial uses in the building. In a project like EINSTEIN TOWER, which rises above a commercial base in a complex planned to include a shopping center of about 11,400 m², understand how the retail will affect the homes: separate entrances, noise, deliveries, parking, management, signage, mechanical installations and rights of use.

On tax, work out purchase tax based on your status: a sole apartment, a replacement apartment, an additional apartment or a purchase by a foreign resident. At these prices, purchase tax can reach substantial sums. Also check financing costs, interest rates, the monthly repayment, the equity ratio, linkage to the index, upgrades and incidental costs. Our guides to purchase tax for foreign residents and mortgages for non-residents give a first picture, but they do not replace advice tailored to you.

Sellers should check capital gains tax on property (mas shevach), exemptions, the linear calculation, the betterment levy, unused building rights and earlier obligations. In buildings with an urban renewal project under way, selling before an agreement is signed, after signing or after a permit is issued can mean different pricing and different tax consequences. Buyers, too, need to know whether future potential is already built into the price. Potential that is not certain is not a promise.

Frequently asked questions

Is North Tel Aviv better for living or for investment?

North Tel Aviv works for both, but not in the same way. As a home, it offers quality of life, schools, parks, the sea nearby and easy access. As an investment, it offers a stable market and strong demand, but high entry prices can reduce the ongoing yield. An investor should decide whether the goal is monthly rent, preserving value, renewal potential or owning a quality asset for the long term.

What is the difference between Ramat Aviv and Neve Avivim?

Ramat Aviv is a broad name covering several sub-areas, among them the original Ramat Aviv, Ramat Aviv Gimel, Green Ramat Aviv and Ramat Aviv Bet, while Neve Avivim is a single established neighborhood built in the 1960s and 1970s, quiet, green and settled. Urban renewal projects are moving forward there, such as the plan approved in 2023 on Yehuda HaNasi Street for 195 apartments in place of 80, so it combines an established market with significant renewal potential.

Why is Einstein Street a focus of new building?

Einstein Street draws new projects because it sits close to Ramat Aviv Mall, Tel Aviv University and the planned Einstein station of the Green Line. Hagag Group's projects on the street are planned to include 515 apartments in six residential buildings and a shopping center of about 11,400 m², EINSTEIN TOWER among them, with 215 apartments in a 28-floor tower and two 13-floor buildings. Ashdar is also active on the street with Ashdar Einstein, as are Azorim and Shikun & Binui.

Will the Sde Dov quarter bring prices down in North Tel Aviv?

Not automatically: the Sde Dov quarter is expected to add significant supply, about 16,000 apartments, but that does not mean prices will simply fall. The effect depends on the pace of sales, delivery dates, price levels, infrastructure, transport, the quality of planning and demand for new apartments by the sea. The quarter may create competition among new projects, but it may also strengthen North Tel Aviv's image as an upscale, renewing part of the city.

What should you check before buying in a new project in North Tel Aviv?

Check the building permit, the land rights, the developer's identity, the project's bank financing, guarantees, specification, indexation terms, timelines, management fees, parking, storage, the building bylaws, common areas and any commercial uses. In urban renewal projects, also check the residents' consents, the planning stage, objections, the risk that the project stalls and the estimated delivery date.

Buying in North Tel Aviv from abroad

North Tel Aviv draws steady interest from investors and buyers living abroad, thanks to its mix of sea, park, university, established neighborhoods, new projects and a luxury market. Foreign residents can buy here, though owning an apartment does not give residency. From abroad, plan for managing the property remotely, tax, financing, a bank account, transferring funds, renting, upkeep, insurance, a power of attorney for your Israeli lawyer, contract language and legal support. Bavli or Ramat Aviv Gimel may suit a buyer who wants a quality apartment in an established area, while Sde Dov may suit one seeking a stake in a new, planned quarter for the long term. Our guide to buying a home in Israel from abroad covers the process.

Treat promised yields, renderings and project marketing with care. Check the original documents, the payment schedule, delivery dates, planning certainty and incidental costs. In luxury deals, management fees, parking, upkeep and shared services can become a significant share of the annual cost. Off-plan, indexation differences and payment dates can move the final cost as much as the price per m².
